World.title: How changes to self-managed super funds are driving new property fears
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalProperty investment How changes to self-managed super funds are driving new property fears Shane Wright July 19, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The housing industry is demanding a review of the government’s changes to borrowing through self-managed super funds, warning thousands of planned new homes will be abandoned while state budgets will suffer a $450 million hit to their bottom line. A Housing Industry Association survey of the sector to be released on Monday shows builders expect up to 67 per cent of 3613 signed home construction contracts financed by limited recourse loans through self-managed super funds (SMSFs) are likely to be ditched because of government policy. The housing industry is warning the government’s crackdown on borrowing through self-managed super funds will hurt the housing market. Glenn Hunt As part of its deal with the Greens to win Senate support for its budget changes to negative gearing and the capital gains tax concession, the government agreed to ban the practice of self-managed funds borrowing for residential property. Formalised in 2011, there have been ongoing concerns about the risk to the financial and superannuation system posed by the practice. An inquiry into the financial system in 2014 initially recommended its abolition while the Council of Financial Regulators – which includes the Reserve Bank and the banking regulator – have also backed changes to the system.



In revealing the ban, Treasurer Jim Chalmers said self-managed funds accounted for less than 1 per cent of total residential property borrowing and less than half a per cent each year. There are about 173,000 homes built over the past 12 months. Related Article Opinion

Property prices A generations-long belief about house prices has just been shattered Shane Wright Senior economics correspondent But HIA chief economist Tim Reardon said its own survey of members had shown the change would ultimately reduce the number of new homes being built and the revenue these would produce for the states. He said builders had 3613 signed contracts with buyers through self-managed fund borrowing arrangements where construction had yet to start. Of those, builders estimate 2415 will be abandoned because of the government’s changes. “These are not hypothetical future investments. They are signed contracts to build homes that builders had expected to construct in the next year,” Reardon said.



“SMSFs do not live in homes. They do not create demand for housing. They do provide capital that finances the construction of new housing. “Restricting one source of investment does not reduce the number of Australians needing somewhere to live.” Reardon said 70 per cent of builders had reported a drop in investor enquiries since the budget’s release in May, with 90 per cent expecting a drop in detached housing starts this year and into 2027. The fall in construction, Reardon said, would equate to a 3.5-5 per cent fall in housing starts with a $450 million fall in GST and stamp duty for state and territory governments. In revealing its negative gearing and CGT changes, the government released Treasury modelling showing they would reduce new home builds by 35,000. This would be offset by a 65,000 increase in homes started because of a $2 billion funding injection for the states and councils to build necessary property infrastructure such as roads and sewerage.



HIA chief economist Tim Reardon says the government should model the impact of its self-managed super fund changes. Louis Trerise Reardon said the government should properly examine the fallout from its SMSF borrowing ban. “Treasury should publish a housing supply impact assessment and cost-benefit analysis consistent with the analysis undertaken for the changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax,” he said. “That assessment should quantify the expected impacts on detached housing, apartment construction, housing affordability and government revenue.” Chalmers has pushed back at claims the SMSF changes will have a substantial impact on the property market, arguing that they do not affect any sale contract exchanged by August 10.



He has also noted that super funds, including SMSFs, could continue to invest in housing and property but not by borrowing against a person’s personal super holdings. The government’s budget tax measures, plus the Reserve Bank’s three interest rate increases this year and record levels of unaffordability in cities such as Brisbane, continue to weigh on the market. Data from Cotality shows auction clearance rates were at 50 per cent at the weekend, with that likely to fall once final sales figures are collated. Coalition housing spokesman Andrew Bragg said on Sunday that lower house prices may be the only way to help young Australians priced out of the property market. “For younger people, some of that should be returned to younger people because prices are too high in Australia for young people who are looking at, in some cases, 15 times a multiple of their salary to buy a first house,” he told the ABC’s Insiders program.



“That is not fair, it is not reasonable. And so that’s why I think our policies must be focused on affordability over the longer term.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: F1 Live: Teenager Antonelli wins Belgian GP; Piastri settles for P5 after collision damage
World.content:
Oscar Piastri’s potential podium dreams lasted for eight whole laps.

After a disappointing qualifying session – marred by a hydraulic leak earlier in the weekend – Piastri started the Belgium Grand Prix in sixth position and seemed unlikely to recreate his 2025 victory at the same circuit.

But the opening lap provided the perfect opportunity. Lewis Hamilton collided with George Russell – sending his former Mercedes teammate into the gravel and ending his race, triggering a safety car. Piastri suddenly found himself in P4 and in contention for a potential podium.

Oscar Piastri ahead of Lewis Hamilton at the Belgian GP. Getty Images

By Lap 8, Piastri was locked in a fierce battle with Charles Leclerc for third, when the Ferrari driver defensively squeezed Piastri outand made contact with the front of the McLaren, sending debris flying.

The impact caused damage to Piastri’s wing and floor.

“He didn’t leave enough space, that could have been a massive crash - Piastri complained over the radio.

The incident was investigated, but the stewards decided to take no action and Leclerc was not penalised.

The Australian dropped places, but persevered– aided by fresh tyres – to climb back up the grid and managed to execute some excellent overtakes. But the McLaren driver ultimately didn’t have the pace to catch Hamilton and finished the race in fifth place.

Hamilton crossed the line in fourth place, however the seven-time world champion and Ferrari are under investigation for an unsafe release, so Piastri could be elevated to fourth place.

Once again it was Kimi Antonelli’s day – the teenager converted pole position to win the Belgian Grand Prix, strengthening his grip on the championship.

After some thrilling battles with Verstappen at the start of the race and in the penultimate lap with Leclerc, Antonelli held on to win his sixth grand prix.

In a post race interview, Antonelli admitted he was “a bit lucky in what happened in terms of the championship” but said he was grateful for win.

Race winner Kimi Antonelli celebrates another win. Getty Images

“That’s why you have to take every opportunity because it can really swing easily, the situation,” he said. “So we just gotta keep performing, keep bringing the result, and seeing what happens at the end of the year.”

Rounding out the podium was Charles Leclerc and Max Verstappen. McLaren’s Lando Norris had an impressive race, fighting his way up from P13 to take the lead of the race after delaying his pitstop. But the 2025 world champion suffered a dreadfully lethargic pitstop of 7.8 seconds, which saw him loose crucial time and drop places.

Fans at the famous Circuit de Spa-Francorchamps also got a nostalgic taste of McLaren inter-team racing, with Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri going wheel-to-wheel. However, it appears the team weren’t keen to implement their famous papaya rules – which states that the two can race each other.

A McLaren engineer interrupted Norris radio to tell him “We don’t want any yo-yo racing with Oscar, I’ll explain why later.”

Ultimately, Sunday’s biggest casualty was George Russell, whose race ended prematurely after the collision with Hamilton.

A devastated George Russell retired from the GP Getty Images

The devastated Mercedes driver told media he got “swallowed up on the straight”, but laid no blame on Hamilton.

“I lost three positions down the straight and the incident was a racing incident. Maybe I could have gone wider, maybe he [Hamilton] could have braked a bit more. I have no words at the moment,” he said in a post-race interview.

Russell’s retirements means the margin to his teammate and rival Antonelli has ballooned to 50 points. Antonelli leads the championship race by 45 points, with Hamilton in second and Russell in third.

The next race is the Hungarian Grand Prix on July 26

World.title: Why the World Cup trophy ceremony might be about to get very awkward
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaFIFA World Cup Why the World Cup trophy ceremony might be about to get very awkward Michael Koziol July 20, 2026 — 4:09am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York New Jersey Stadium: There are no prizes for guessing who Donald Trump is supporting in the World Cup final. The US president - a sports fan, but not a soccer aficionado - has long been close with Argentina’s right-wing libertarian leader, Javier Milei. Trump and Milei at the White House last October. AP “He’s MAGA all the way,” Trump said when the two met at the White House last year, just a few days before Anthony Albanese’s visit. He even handed Argentina a $US20 billion ($28.6b) emergency credit swap, although little of it was ultimately used. Milei has been something of a regular in Washington, too - he joined Elon Musk on stage at the Conservative Political Action Conference last April, where he gifted the world’s richest man a chainsaw for use in cutting government largesse.



So there’s a fairly strong bromance between the two conservative presidents. But one can’t say the same for Spain, which is in the Trump doghouse. At the NATO summit in Turkey earlier this month, Trump called Spain a “terrible partner” and told secretary-general Mark Rutte: “Spain doesn’t agree to anything, and you ⁠shouldn’t carry them.” FIFA President Gianni Infantino and Donald Trump present the FIFA Club World Cup trophy to Chelsea last year. Getty Images He also instructed his treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, to sever all US trade with Spain. “I don’t want anything to do with Spain.” And yet, trade continues as normal, as it did the last time Trump made such threats. And by the end of the NATO conference, he had softened a lot, telling reporters on Air Force One that Madrid “came back all the way today”.



The main source of Trump’s beef with Spain is its refusal to sign up to a new NATO target - at Trump’s insistence - of spending 5 per cent of gross domestic product on defence. That comprises 3.5 per cent on core military spending and another 1.5 per cent on related matters such as road or cyber infrastructure. Madrid secured an exemption that would see its defence expenditure capped at 2.1 per cent of GDP. Javier Milei, Argentina’s president, right, presents a chainsaw to Elon Musk at a conservative conference in Washington. Bloomberg Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez - who, unlike Argentina’s Milei, is attending the World Cup final - is a left-wing leader who heads the Spanish Socialist Workers’ Party and is also the president of Socialist International. He has recognised a Palestinian state, described Israel’s campaign in Gaza as “genocide”, and denounced Trump’s capture of then Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro as a violation of international law. In short, Sánchez is something of an anti-Trump.



Which will make it all the more awkward if Trump - who is supposed to be doing the honours at the end of today’s match - has to hand the World Cup trophy to Spain. One outspoken Spanish player, Borja Iglesias, joked that he would shake Trump’s hand at the ceremony if only to avoid jail. Spanish player Borja Iglesias said he would shake Trump’s hand to avoid jail. Getty Images “I don’t want to go to prison,” he said. “I hope to greet him at a time when we are all very happy, and that it passes very quickly, and I can forget about it.” There’s also the question of what kind of welcome Trump will get from the Spanish fans in the house, and what kind of spectacle he will be on stage.



Last year, when Trump was on hand to present the FIFA Club World Cup trophy to winners Chelsea, he lingered on stage awkwardly and even took part in Chelsea’s customary celebrations. His buddy, FIFA president Gianni Infantino, eventually pulled him away.

World.title: FIFA World Cup 2026 LIVE updates: Lionel Messi’s Argentina meet Spain in final
World.content:
The last stop on train line that is the world’s biggest sporting event but could also be a tournament of geopolitics, of economic greed, of drama on and off the pitch, and of emotion ... dreadful surprise and beautiful shock have underpinned the past five weeks. Gianni Infantino had promised every match of the 2026 World Cup would be a Super Bowl in itself. Well, this morning’s final is anticipated to draw an audience at least 10 times the size of the Super Bowl. So, job done.

The teams at the centre? Spain and Argentina. Two reigning continental champions, of Europe and South America. Spain, unbeaten in 37 games, are a team in service to the collective and to the ball. Argentina, the defending world champions, are in service to their 39-year-old talisman Lionel Messi. They have never met in a World Cup knockout game. In fact, they have met only once on this stage: in the group phase of 1966. You could argue this meeting is 60 years in the making.

Kick-off is at 5am AEST. We’ll be with you for the build-up, the game, and all the wash-up.

World.title: ‘A bloody good feeling’: Essendon bask in the glow of landing a win, climbing off the bottom
World.content:
AFL Briefing SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘A bloody good feeling’: Essendon bask in the glow of landing a win, climbing off the bottom Oliver Caffrey , Ed Jackson , Nick Smart and Scott Spits Updated July 20, 2026 — 12:26am ,first published 4:18pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

In today’s AFL Briefing, your daily wrap of footy news: Western Bulldogs heaped more pressure on Gold Coast with a nine-point win.

Hawthorn dined out on lowly Richmond at the MCG on Sunday.

Carlton forward Harry McKay suffered bone bruising and a minor tear in his meniscus against Collingwood. Dons delight: Bombers end losing streak Oliver Caffrey An elated Dean Solomon has described Essendon’s stunning three-point upset of inconsistent GWS as a “bloody good feeling”. Having won just one of their previous 30 games, the Bombers finally played with a sense of urgency to give Solomon his first win in his 10th match as a caretaker coach, which includes three at Gold Coast in 2017.



Leading at every break, Essendon gave up their advantage twice in a frantic final term but hit back through clutch goals to Sullivan Robey and Peter Wright. Sheer wonder: Jacob Farrow of the Bombers. Getty Images With a wildcard spot still up for grabs, the Giants desperately tried to reclaim the lead in the dying stages, but Essendon hung on for a famous win - 10.7 (67) to 8.16 (64) - amid scenes of delirium in front of a small, but vocal crowd at Marvel Stadium. It was Essendon’s first win since beating Melbourne in Gather Round in Adelaide on April 11, while they hadn’t won a game in Victoria since May 2025. The Bombers, who were ravaged by Brisbane last Sunday and had lost 12-straight matches, were given virtually no hope of matching it with the red-hot Giants.



“It’s a bloody good feeling,” Solomon said. Pumped: Dean Solomon with Zach Merrett. Getty Images “Our footy club’s been on its knees for a period of time, and the footy world’s jumped on that, and they enjoy us sitting at the bottom. “We’ve felt that, and we don’t like that, so to push back a little bit and get one win, albeit one win, I’m just really happy for these players.” The result continued GWS’s baffling trend of struggling against lower-ranked opposition whilst also dismantling last year’s grand finalists Brisbane and Geelong, and rampaging ladder-leaders Fremantle, amid their previous seven games.



As well as the Bombers, GWS have dropped matches to St Kilda (twice) and West Coast. “It was incredibly disappointing,” Giants coach Adam Kingsley said. “The messaging around our consistency, our ability to perform against every team in the competition, not just those who were above us.” In a further concern for the Giants, they lost captain Toby Greene to a serious-looking quad injury in the third quarter that will almost certainly mean he misses the Sydney derby against the Swans next Saturday. Further delighting the home crowd, former Essendon forward Jake Stringer endured a horror match in front of goal to finish with 0.7 on a wayward night for the Giants.



View post on X The only concern for Essendon was young star Nate Caddy, who was sent to hospital due to an elevated heart rate. Caddy, who recently re-signed until the end of 2031 in a massive boost for the battling Bombers, didn’t return to the ground after quarter-time. Solomon revealed Caddy had been able to leave hospital, but would undergo further tests during the week.



“To do it without him is sad in one instance, but it’s also a pretty super effort from this group,” Solomon said. The result could prove costly for GWS, who would have jumped into 10th and a wildcard spot, had they beaten the Bombers. It also lifted Essendon to 17th, sending Richmond to the bottom of the ladder. View post on X AAP



Bulldogs pile more misery on Suns in nine-point win Gold Coast coach Damien Hardwick believes his team is falling short in critical moments after a nine-point loss to the Western Bulldogs. The 11.11 (77) to 9.14 (68) defeat on Sunday at a blustery People First Stadium was the Suns’ eighth consecutive defeat, further eroding their slim hopes of sneaking into a top 10 position. For the Bulldogs, the victory cements them in seventh and gives them breathing space over the chasing pack in and around that crucial 10th position on the ladder.



Gold Coast’s loss came despite the Suns having 91 more disposals, nine more clearances and 11 more inside 50s than the visitors. Roaring with delight: Ed Richards of the Bulldogs. AFL Photos Hardwick conceded a 10-minute period in the third quarter, in which the Bulldogs kicked five-goals-to-none, was symptomatic of a wider issue in his team of not capitalising when the game is on the line. “We won clearances by a lot,” Hardwick said. “We smacked them in contested ball. We smacked them in tackles. We smacked them in inside 50s. “We lost the game.



“At the end of the day, the game looks like a Suns game for 80 per cent (but) for 20 per cent it comes out of reach. “Credit to the Bulldogs, they defended quite well, but we had shots on goal that we should have scored, and we didn’t score. “Our guys are paid to kick goals, and unfortunately, if you don’t, it comes back to haunt you in a close-finishing game.” Arthur Jones shows some dash for the Bulldogs. AFL Photos The Suns’ lack of cutting edge was epitomised by an off day in front of goal for Ben King, with the key forward finishing with 1.4.



Christian Petracca did kick two goals but was also responsible for a crucial third-quarter clanger which allowed Rory Lobb to score during that match-winning burst by the Bulldogs. In a team shorn of Tom Liberatore (soreness) and Riley Garcia (hamstring tightness) and missing Bailey Dale for the first time since 2020, superstar Marcus Bontempelli delivered where the Suns couldn’t - in crucial moments. The Bulldogs’ captain kicked three goals, including two in the first quarter, while Matthew Kennedy celebrated the birth of his second child with three majors of his own. Bailey Humphrey was busy with 29 disposals and 765 metres gained while for the Suns, Petracca and Leo Lombard kicked two goals each with Touk Miller (39 disposals, five tackles, nine clearances) and Matt Rowell (26 disposals, 11 tackles and eight clearances) dominant in midfield. “To come in at halftime and settle, and then have a third quarter like we did was impressive by the boys,” Bulldogs coach Luke Beveridge said.



“It probably got a little bit shaky right at the end, but really pleased with the outcome ... we’ve won a few important ones interstate, and this is just as important as any.” Gold Coast travel to face Carlton next week while the Bulldogs are at home against Richmond. AAP Watson and Lewis pile on goals as Hawthorn destroy lowly Tigers



Hawthorn have returned to third on the AFL ladder with a major percentage boost thanks to a brutal 70-point demolition of lowly Richmond at the MCG. The Hawks went into the clash sitting sixth after other results this weekend, but their 18.14 (122) to 6.16 (52) thrashing of the Tigers made a major statement and lifted them back into the top four. Sunday’s final margin flattered Richmond after they kicked several late consolation goals once Hawthorn eased off in the final term. They had led by as much as 87 points during the third quarter. Pointing the way to a win: Hawthorn’s Nick Watson. AFL Photos



Uncontracted Hawk Mitch Lewis dominated up forward with five goals, all in the first half. Goalsneak Nick Watson matched him by also kicking five goals in a stunning first-half performance. The only injury concern for the Hawks was Jack Ginnivan, who was pulled at half-time with the club citing “back soreness.” For Richmond, it was a sour way to commemorate triple premiership player Dion Prestia’s 250th game. The only positive was veteran Tom Lynch finally kicking his 500th goal late in the final term after several weeks stuck on 499.



Tiger Taj Hotton failed to finish the game after suffering an ankle injury, while fellow youngster Steely Green finished the match under a HIA. Jarman Impey is fleet of foot and kicks a running goal on Sunday. AFL Photos Watson, who was back from a two-week injury lay-off, picked up where he left off by kicking the first goal mid-way through the first term after a pedestrian start by both teams. He was able to slot a second goal in the opening quarter but was upstaged by a rampaging Lewis, who kicked three in the first 30 minutes. Lewis would have had four goals by quarter-time had his set shot after the siren not narrowly missed.



But Lewis didn’t have to wait too long for his fourth – which came early in the second term – on his way to five majors. The hapless Tigers went goalless in the first term, and were cruelly denied what would have been a brilliant Seth Campbell goal late in the term by an ARC overrule. Richmond supporters had to wait until the ninth minute of the second quarter to cheer their side’s first major, which came courtesy of Patrick Retschko. View post on X The Tigers had two in a minute after Mykelti Lefau kicked truly, but any joy was short-lived as Hawthorn piled on the next six.



Hawthorn led by a whopping 63 points at the main break, their largest halftime lead in five seasons under coach Sam Mitchell. The Hawks threatened to blow the margin beyond 100 points in the third term before the Tigers were able to make the scoreline more respectable by the final siren. AAP McKay could play through injury for Carlton



Scott Spits, Danny Russell Carlton forward Harry McKay suffered bone bruising and a minor tear in his meniscus after an awkward clash that commentators described as innocuous-looking against Collingwood at the MCG on Saturday night. Scans on Sunday confirmed the prognosis for McKay, who was forced from the field early in the Blues’ 21-point loss to the Magpies that has effectively ruled Carlton out of the wildcard race. McKay bumped knees with teammate Sam Walsh early in the first quarter. Despite the benign nature of the impact, McKay was unable to run and took himself from the ground. Harry McKay suffered bone bruising and a meniscus tear. AFL Photos via Getty Images



His absence left the Carlton forward line short on potency. The Blues said midfielder Adam Cerra, who experienced hamstring tightness and was withdrawn in the second quarter, had not suffered a strain. Carlton said McKay and Cerra would be tested and both may play against Gold Coast at Marvel Stadium next Saturday. Carlton’s caretaker coach Josh Fraser would not be drawn on the severity of McKay’s injury. “Those ones can sometimes look worse than what they appear,” Fraser said after the match. “I don’t know. I haven’t received any more information on it.” Fox Footy commentator David King was perplexed by McKay’s injury. “No one is questioning whether he is injured or not,” he said.



“We are just wondering if it is a pain issue or is it a structural issue. When it has such an influence on the group, it changes six or seven roles in the team, and they were right in the game.” Collingwood coach Craig McRae agreed McKay’s absence for most of the night aided an undermanned Magpies back line. World.title: Families feel pressures as school costs rise. Grandparents are helping
World.content:
NationalEducation Families feel pressures as school costs rise. Grandparents are helping Jackson Graham July 20, 2026 — 12:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

More than half of families with children at private schools, or who are considering enrolling them, say they are under significant cost pressure, according to new research by the sector’s peak body, which finds most are saving for at least three years to afford the fees. The data, released by Independent Schools Australia on Monday, is from a national sample of 629 families of children at independent schools, and 879 families who are weighing up this option, surveyed between March and April this year. Sandra Masel pays for her grandson’s fees at a private school in Melbourne’s inner east. Joe Armao It found 53 per cent of families were under significant financial pressure, and 57 per cent saved for three or more years for the fees, while 10 per cent saved for more than a decade. Three-quarters of participants said they are adjusting household budgets to afford it, including almost half by reducing holiday spending and cutting non-essentials. A smaller portion of 28 per cent were also cutting essentials, and 18 per cent of respondents were reducing their housing costs.



Related Article Education The biggest losers set to miss out on millions due to private school cash cuts “These are real trade-offs that affect how families live, save and plan. The evidence shows how strongly families value their chosen school. It also shows that the financial commitment to education is not unlimited,” the ISA report finds. It comes as new figures also show Victorian grandparents are financially helping one in 10 families with their child’s schooling, including at government schools, for costs including camps and uniforms. Grandparents in public schooling contribute $1234 annually, compared to $1676 in the Catholic sector and $5593 in the private sector, the Resolve Strategic research commissioned by education bonds company Futurity Investment Group found. Separate research from Independent Schools Australia also found earlier this year that one in five families at private schools received help from other family members for fees. In Victoria, an analysis by this masthead found that schools that had put up their fees had increased them by 5 per cent in the private sector, and many Catholic schools increased their fees by even higher percentages.



Xavier College principal Lee MacMaster said that anecdotally, the school is aware that grandparents in the school community assist with fees. “However, we do not keep data on this,” he said. “We are very grateful for the support of grandparents in supporting the ongoing education of their grandsons at the college.” Some grandparents help pay Xavier College’s school fees. Eddie Jim Sandra Masel, 83, pays the fees for her grandson to attend a private school in Melbourne’s inner east. Masel attended a private school; so did her children, who now face higher living costs and different employment situations than she did at their age. “I figured my grandchild should have the same opportunity, and I can afford it, and they can’t. So it’s a no-brainer, really. I wanted to give them the choice,” Masel said. “Whoever has more money, I think should contribute. There’s no point in making your children wait, and they get the money when they don’t need it any more. They always say you should give with a warm hand, not a cold hand.”



Related Article Exclusive

Education Rooftop tennis courts and Olympic pools: private schools’ multimillion-dollar arms race Masel does not pay for any school camps or extra activities, and said it was completely up to her son’s family where they choose to send their child to school. She said there was no doubt that families faced higher costs of living relative to wages than when she and her late husband paid for their children’s fees themselves. “There’s no question about that. After tax dollars, how can a working couple pay $50,000 a year for each child if they have three kids? It doesn’t stack up.” However, Grandparents Australia director Anne McLeish said there was a worrying trend of older people feeling pressure to pay, especially for activities such as camps at government schools. She was concerned that grandparents could put themselves under too much pressure to contribute to private school fees. “I think that they need to think very carefully about the sacrifices they make to their quality of life to prop up funding education,” McLeish said.



“Grandparents are seduced by the idea that the children need the best quality education, and it’s expensive. It’s not necessarily expensive at all. The best quality education can be determined by looking at the school options and matching the school culture to the family culture.” Families paid $410.3 million to Victorian government schools, the most in Australia, as part of voluntary fees, charges and contributions in 2024, according to the most recent data available from the Australian Curriculum and Assessment Reporting Authority. Jan Dods is paying for her granddaughter Calypso to go on a school ski excursion this term. Ruby Alexander. Eighty-two-year-old Jan Dods has a daughter and a son, and seven grandchildren. Her son sent his children to private schools on part-scholarships, while her daughter’s children attend government schools. Dods’ daughter is a single mother, and Dods has contributed to the grandchildren’s education on this side of the family, including occasionally paying for uniforms and higher costs such as educational trips to China, a young leader trip to Costa Rica and Nicaragua and an art trip to New York City.



Related Article Exclusive

Education ‘Not all about chasing ATARs’: VCE subjects show a clear public-private divide She will fund her youngest granddaughter Calypso to go on a school ski camp to Mount Hotham this term. “I determined that I would try to fill the gaps so that these children would have as much opportunity in the way of stimulating educational experiences as possible,” Dods said. She believed it could last longer than physical gifts. “Education is something that you’ve got in your head and everything else can go,” Dods said. “I have no intention of having a lot of money when I die. I want to give it to them now. They might not need it, or I might not need it. I might not have enough, but I’m being pretty frugal.” The Morning Edition newsletter is our guide to the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. Sign up here.

World.title: Five key takeaways from Pauline Hanson’s Spotlight special
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPauline Hanson Five key takeaways from Pauline Hanson’s Spotlight special William Davis Updated July 19, 2026 — 11:44pm ,first published 10:44pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Pauline Hanson said she loved the idea of mass deportations for Australia, and suggested Tommy Robinson would be welcome Down Under if she became prime minister in a friendly meeting with the convicted criminal. During Seven’s hour-long Spotlight special that tracked Hanson during what she described as a “fact-finding mission” to the UK, the One Nation leader claimed the end of the White Australia Policy had led to problems for Australia, and added she didn’t regret anything – including her push for a “monoculture” and warning the country was at risk of being “swamped” by Asians. Pauline Hanson Spotlight episode on Channel 7. Seven “It’s been really good to come over here on this trip and see what’s happening because it’s really making me determined,” Hanson remarked while walking through the London Borough of Tower Hamlets. Its population is nearly 40 per cent Muslim, the highest proportion of anywhere in England. “I was determined beforehand, but more so now because seeing what’s happened here, I’m going to fight it … I’m not going to have it happen in Australia.”



Here are five key takeaways from the program that aired on Sunday night. Hanson wants to see mass deportations in Australia In the program, Hanson expresses support for radical mass deportations pushed by a fringe party to the right of Reform in the UK. She had, according to journalist Liam Bartlett, been supposed to meet with UK Reform leader and Brexit architect Nigel Farage, however the meeting was scuppered following his decision to resign as an MP in the days prior amid an investigation into his acceptance of funds. Hanson did meet with Restore leader Rupert Lowe who is pushing for mass deportations across the UK. Lowe has called for the removal of 1.8 to 2 million of the UK’s nearly 70 million population.



“Oh, I love it,” she said when asked for her view on mass deportations, confirming she’s “very much on the same page” as the British politician. She did not explain how such a plan would be carried out. Former Neighbours star turned right-wing commentator Holly Valance made a brief cameo during the meeting. Robinson would be welcome to visit Australia under One Nation Pauline Hanson Spotlight episode on Channel 7. Seven



Later in the program Hanson met Robinson, a renowned English racist and convicted criminal whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon. Farage has distanced himself from Robinson and called him a “thug”, while Robinson’s appearance on Karl Stefanovic’s podcast led to Nine axing the Today show host’s lucrative contract. The duo smiled at each other warmly during the meeting, with Robinson saying “the path has been paved by people like Pauline Hanson.” He told her he would like to come to Australia, but falsely claims he’d never tried as he thought his convictions would prevent him getting a visa. He had visas rejected on two previous occasions. “Wait until I’m in, you won’t have … ” she says before being cut off, seemingly from adding “a problem.”



Later asked why she would associate with a man considered too extreme for Reform in the UK, she immediately became defensive. “Why wouldn’t I talk to the man?” Hanson said. “I will say and do what I want to, and I will talk to people if I feel … [I should spend time with] to learn from. “That’s the first time I’ve met Tommy Robinson, and I don’t regret meeting with him.” There’s nothing at all Hanson regrets



Pauline Hanson Spotlight episode on Channel 7. Seven The One Nation leader was later asked if there was anything at all she did regret from her 30 years in public life. “Nothing I can think of,” she said. She specifically defended her calls for a monoculture, describing Islam as a “disease” and early claim Australia was at risk of being “swamped by Asians”. “I will apologise if I’m wrong, but I said it for a reason at the time,” Hanson responded.



“I put my head on the chopping block all the time, and I stand up against the establishment and I say what’s really on my mind.” Barnaby Joyce is on message for One Nation Editor's pick Analysis

Pauline Hanson Hanson knew she had questions to answer. She ran for cover One Nation’s prized Coalition defector stayed on message, and brushed off remarks he’d made in 2017 suggesting Australia would go “down the toilet” if Hanson’s party ever formed government. “Things have changed,” Joyce said. “If people don’t agree with my decision to join One Nation, then I imagine they won’t vote for me, and that’ll be the end of the story.



“You know who else is changing their position … voters.” He suggested there were other big names hoping to join One Nation, and said his boss did have the intellectual capacity to be Prime Minister. Hanson later quipped she didn’t have an ambition to lead the country, but would do it if it were a “necessity”. Joyce reiterated that he did not believe in multiculturalism, and said the Bondi terrorist attack had changed his views on Islam. Hanson cites end of White Australia policy



Asked by Robinson to explain the Australian immigration system and why the country had accepted “violent” people from other places, Hanson pointed to the end of the White Australia Policy. “It started in 1973 with Gough Whitlam. So they opened up and got rid of the White Australia policy,” she said. Related Article Updated

Political leadership ‘Do not apologise for being white’: Hanson takes aim at privilege and trans rights “Then they started bringing in the different migrants, and a lot of them couldn’t speak English, but they learned to speak English.” Hanson then said without evidence many immigrants were moving to Australia to rort the welfare system.



This masthead previously published those comments about the White Australia Policy, and she attacked the reporting on social media as “fake news”. “Never ever have I advocated [for reintroducing the White Australia Policy], and I don’t believe in it as well,” she said in a video published to Facebook. “Yes, I’ve been strong on immigration, bringing the right people in the country in a measured way, and people who want to assimilate and be Australians.” Get the day’s breaking news, entertainment ideas and a long read to enjoy.
